# RealHunt: full reference

> RealHunt (https://realhunt.co) is where foreigners find, check and buy property: homes for sale around the world, each checked by a person and graded from 70 to 98 against every other home on the site, with buying rules, taxes and costs by country. It is not an estate agent; every home links to its original listing. Legal and tax notes are general information, not advice.

Updated 2026-11-14. 591 homes. Short index: https://realhunt.co/llms.txt. You may quote this content with a link to the page it comes from.

## Who we are

RealHunt is run by Equinox Investment Group LLC, 30 N Gould St Ste N, Sheridan, WY 82801, United States. Founder: Carlos de Ory Gordillo. Contact: hello@realhunt.co.

### How RealHunt makes money

Buyers pay nothing. Resale homes are not for sale through RealHunt: we link to the original listing. On new builds, RealHunt earns a fee from the developer only if a buyer it introduced buys. Nobody pays to be listed or to rank higher, and sponsored cards are marked as sponsored.

## How the RealHunt score works

A person looks at every home before it goes up. Homes that need major work, ruins, bare land and listings with one photo are turned down. That is why the grade starts at 70: a home on RealHunt has already passed.

The grade then compares the home with every other home on the site, from 70 to 98. The home pages, the country pages and the front page are all ordered by this grade, best first. Votes and saves only move the buyer-interest sub-score; nobody pays to rank higher.

### The 11 sub-scores (0 to 100)

- Price: How cheap it is next to every other home here and in its country
- Price per m²: How little you pay per square metre
- Space: Size of the house
- Move-in condition: Renovated or ready to live in scores more; homes that need work score less
- Extras: Garden, terrace, pool, sauna, fireplace, views, land and more
- Sea & lakes: How close it is to the sea or a lake
- Good weather: Good-weather days a year where the home is: a high of 18–33 °C, dry, light wind (climate normals)
- Airport: Nearest airport with scheduled flights: 20 km or less scores 100, then it drops evenly to 0 at 200 km or more
- Buying costs: Taxes and fees to buy in this country: lower scores more
- Listing detail: Photos, size and rooms published, verified by us
- Buyer interest: Views and saves from RealHunt buyers

### What the score is not

It is not a survey or a valuation. Photos can flatter and listings go out of date. Before you buy anything, get an independent inspection and a local lawyer or notary. If a home is sold or wrong, use the report button on its page.

## Buying a home in Albania: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes, apartments and houses freely; agricultural land is excluded. Title risk from communist-era confiscations.

Costs on top of the price
1.3-1.9% · Notary 0.23-0.35% + lawyer 0.1-0.5% + agent 1-2%; transfer tax (0.5-3%) is paid by the seller (GPG, 2021).

Yearly property tax
Local property tax ~0.05% of cadastral value (about EUR 75/yr on EUR 150k).

Tax on rental income
Flat 15% on rental income, including short-term, declared via the DIVA platform.

What holiday rentals earn
No sourced STR gross yield. Airbtics 2025: national occupancy 56%, Durres 53%, Tirana 62%; AirROI (via internationalinvestment.biz, Dec 2025) Tirana ~40% occupancy, ~US$6,600/yr typical income.

Long-term rent yield
4.2-6.1 (GPG Sep 2022: Tirana 6.09, Vlore 4.81, Durres 4.51)% gross

Holiday-rental rules
No licence or business tax ID (NIPT) required for individuals; income must be declared on DIVA, with new reporting obligations from 2026.

## Buying a home in Bali: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
No freehold (Hak Milik) for foreigners: leasehold, Hak Pakai (right-to-use, 30 yrs + renewals), or HGB title via a PT PMA foreign-owned company.

Costs on top of the price
6.5-18% · BPHTB transfer tax 5% + notary 1-2.5% + legal 0.5-1.5% (GPG: 6.5-9%); new developer units add 11% PPN/VAT (stack ~17-18% without the 2026 PPN-DTP incentive, ~6-9% with it). Plain leasehold deals mostly notary/legal.

Yearly property tax
PBB land & building tax, up to ~0.5% of assessed NJOP-based value (low hundreds USD on a $300k villa).

Tax on rental income
Non-residents: 20% withholding on gross rent (10% possible under a tax treaty); PT PMA companies 22% corporate tax.

Holiday-rental yield
8-15% gross

What holiday rentals earn
Gross. Industry-quoted range for well-located villas (Global Investments guide 8-15%; Kinnara.Asia blended ~8.5% via Paradyse Homes). Operating costs typically 35-45% of revenue, net ~5-10%. Sources are agents/developers, treat as optimistic.

Holiday-rental rules
Short-term renting requires a Pondok Wisata (homestay) licence; foreigners cannot hold it personally and need a PT PMA with the right KBLI code plus PBG/SLF building permits.

## Buying a home in Bulgaria: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes, buildings and apartments, with rights similar to locals; per GPG, foreigners can't own land directly, so a Bulgarian company is the usual route.

Costs on top of the price
3.2-8.5% · Transfer tax 0.1-3% (municipal; Sofia 2.5%) + notary 0.1-1.5% + legal 0.5-1% + agent 2.5-3%.

Yearly property tax
0.01-0.45% of the property's tax value plus a municipal garbage fee.

Tax on rental income
Non-residents: 10% final tax on gross rent, paid quarterly, no deductions.

What holiday rentals earn
No sourced STR gross yield found.

Long-term rent yield
3.8-4.7 (GPG Q3 2026: Burgas 4.72, Varna 4.29, Sofia 3.84, national 4.27)% gross

Holiday-rental rules
Tourist accommodation must be categorised or registered with the municipality under the Tourism Act; tourist tax BGN 0.20-3.00 per night.

## Buying a home in Canada: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Mostly not for now: a federal ban stops non-Canadians from buying homes in cities and larger towns until January 1, 2027, with exceptions such as work permit holders and spouses of citizens or permanent residents. The ban does not cover rural areas and small towns, and the government has said it does not plan simply to extend it, but a replacement is being studied.

Costs on top of the price
1.5-4% · Buyers usually pay provincial land transfer tax on a sliding scale (Ontario: 0.5% up to $55,000 and 1% from $55,000 to $250,000), legal fees of about $500 to $1,500, title insurance of about $250 and an inspection of $300 to $1,000, while the seller usually pays the agents; foreign buyers also pay Ontario's 25% non-resident speculation tax anywhere in Ontario and British Columbia's 20% additional tax in Metro Vancouver and four other regions.

Yearly property tax
Property tax is set by each city as a share of assessed value, from about 0.3% in Vancouver to 2.12% in Saint John in 2026.

Tax on rental income
Non-residents have 25% of gross rent withheld, but they can file a Section 216 return to pay tax on net rent instead, and Form NR6 lets the agent withhold on net rent.

## Buying a home in Cyprus: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
EU citizens buy without restrictions. Non-EU buyers need permission from the Council of Ministers, applied for through the District Officer, and are normally limited to one home or a plot of up to 4,014 m².

Costs on top of the price
2.5-3.5% · Land Registry transfer fees of 3% up to €85,000, 5% to €170,000 and 8% above, halved for resales without VAT (1.5%, 2.5% and 4%); stamp duty abolished from 1 January 2026; lawyer about 1% plus VAT; small Land Registry charges.

Yearly property tax
There is no annual national property tax (abolished in 2017); owners pay municipal fees of about €90 to €300 a year, plus sewerage and local authority charges.

Tax on rental income
Non-residents pay income tax on Cyprus rental income at 20% to 35% after deducting 20% of the gross rent and loan interest, plus a 2.65% health contribution (GHS); the special defence contribution does not apply to them.

## Buying a home in Denmark: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Without Danish domicile or 5 years of past residence you need permission from the Department of Civil Affairs (Civilstyrelsen); EU/EEA citizens who live and are registered in Denmark can buy a permanent home without permission by signing a declaration to the Land Registration Court. Holiday homes (sommerhuse) need permission, which is only given to people with particularly strong ties to Denmark, such as many years of holidays there.

Costs on top of the price
1.5-3% · Registration fee on the deed (tinglysningsafgift) of DKK 1,850 plus 0.6% of the price, about 1% for a buyer's lawyer, and, if you borrow, a mortgage registration fee of DKK 1,825 plus 1.25% of the loan; the seller normally pays the agent.

Yearly property tax
Owners pay property value tax (ejendomsværdiskat) of 0.51% on 80% of the official valuation (1.4% above DKK 9.2 million) plus municipal land tax (grundskyld) at a rate set by each municipality, capped at 30 per mille of the land value.

Tax on rental income
A non-resident who rents out a Danish home is taxed in Denmark on the profit under the ordinary Danish rules; staying in Denmark more than 3 months at a time or 180 days a year, or working there, makes you fully tax liable.

## Buying a home in the Dominican Republic: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes. Foreigners have the same rights as Dominican citizens to buy land and homes, with no restrictions.

Costs on top of the price
4.25-7% · The buyer pays a 3% transfer tax (0% for qualifying first purchases under CONFOTUR tourism incentives), legal fees of about 1-2% and notary fees of about 0.25-1%, plus registration costs, while the seller pays the 2-3% agent fee.

Yearly property tax
The yearly IPI tax is 1% of the part of a person's total Dominican property value, as assessed by the tax office DGII, above RD$10,695,494 in 2026, so a single cheap home is often below the threshold.

Tax on rental income
Rent paid abroad to a non-resident is generally subject to 27% withholding.

## Buying a home in France: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes. Foreigners can buy property in France without major restrictions, and non-EU buyers do not need a permit, although the paperwork can take longer.

Costs on top of the price
7-8.5% · Transfer taxes (droits de mutation) of about 5.8%, or about 6.3% in departments that raised their rate for 2025 to March 2028; notary fee (émoluments) on a sliding scale from 3.87% down to 0.799% plus 20% VAT, about 1.3% on a €150,000 home; land security contribution (contribution de sécurité immobilière) 0.10%; disbursements (débours) of about €800 to €1,200; the agent fee is usually built into the advertised price (FAI) and paid by the seller, sometimes shared.

Yearly property tax
Owners pay an annual property tax (taxe foncière) set by the local authorities, and owners of a furnished second home also pay housing tax (taxe d'habitation), which some communes raise by a surcharge of 5% to 60%.

Tax on rental income
Non-residents pay French income tax on French rental income at a minimum rate of 20% (30% above about €27,500), plus social charges of 17.2%, or 7.5% for people covered by social security in another EU/EEA country or Switzerland.

## Buying a home in Georgia: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes, residential and commercial property freely; agricultural land is reserved for citizens.

Costs on top of the price
0.6-1.1% · No transfer tax or stamp duty; registry fee 50-200 GEL, notary under 0.1%, legal 0.5-1%; agent 2-3% if buyer-paid.

Yearly property tax
Only for tax residents: 0.05-1% of value depending on household income; non-residents generally exempt.

Tax on rental income
5% of gross rent on residential property (long- or short-term), residents and non-residents alike.

What holiday rentals earn
No sourced STR gross yield. Airbtics (Feb 2025-Jan 2026): Batumi 53% occupancy, ADR US$43, median revenue ~US$8k/yr, listings +46% YoY, graded D and ranked in the lowest 4% for STR yield in Eastern Europe.

Long-term rent yield
7.2-7.3 (GPG Q3 2026: Tbilisi 7.23, Batumi 7.28)% gross

Holiday-rental rules
No specific short-term rental licence found in sources; the 5% rental tax applies.

## Buying a home in Germany: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes. There are no restrictions on foreigners buying property in Germany, though non-EU buyers usually need a bigger down payment to get a loan.

Costs on top of the price
5-8.5% · Real estate transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer) of 3.5% to 6.5% depending on the state (3.5% in Bavaria, 6.5% in Brandenburg, North Rhine-Westphalia, Saarland and Schleswig-Holstein), plus notary and land registry fees (Notar- und Grundbuchkosten) of about 1.5-2%; if the seller hired the agent, the buyer pays half the commission by law, which is extra.

Yearly property tax
Owners pay property tax (Grundsteuer), calculated since 2025 as assessed value x a tax rate x a municipal multiplier (Hebesatz) that each municipality sets.

Tax on rental income
Non-resident owners are taxed in Germany on net rental income at the normal progressive income tax rates, but without the basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag).

## Buying a home in Greece: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes. Buyers from outside the EU and EFTA need a permit to buy in designated border areas (parts of northern Greece and eastern Aegean islands such as the Dodecanese and Rhodes). The government has announced a 15% transfer tax for non-EU buyers of homes from 1 January 2027, not yet final in September 2026.

Costs on top of the price
5.5-7% · Transfer tax 3.09% of the price or the taxable value, whichever is higher; notary about 0.8-1% plus VAT; land registry fees about 0.5-0.7%; lawyer 1-2% plus VAT; if an agent is used, the buyer usually pays a commission of 1-3% plus VAT on top.

Yearly property tax
Owners on 1 January pay the unified property tax (ENFIA), calculated per property from its location, size, age and official zone value, with an extra charge if total Greek property exceeds €500,000.

Tax on rental income
Non-residents pay Greek tax on Greek rental income at 15% up to €12,000, 25% to €24,000, 35% to €36,000 and 45% above, after a flat 5% deduction for expenses.

## Buying a home in Italy: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes for EU citizens; non-EU buyers need reciprocity (US, UK, Canada, Australia qualify).

Costs on top of the price
4-15% · Registration tax 9% on a second home (resale), or VAT on new builds; notary 1-2% + legal ~1% + agent ~3% (GPG roundtrip 10-18%).

Yearly property tax
IMU 0.4-1.06% on second homes (on cadastral value).

Tax on rental income
Optional flat 'cedolare secca' on short lets: 21% for one property, 26% from the second.

What holiday rentals earn
No sourced STR gross yield found. Cheap Italian homes are usually old stock in depopulating towns, not new builds.

Long-term rent yield
5.0-8.8 (GPG Q3 2026: national 6.61, Catania 8.75, Palermo 7.84, Milan 4.97)% gross

Holiday-rental rules
Every tourist let needs a national CIN code shown on listings and at the property; from the 3rd property it is treated as a business (VAT registration).

## Buying a home in Japan: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes. Foreigners can buy freehold land and homes on the same terms as Japanese citizens, even on a tourist visa, though buying does not give a visa or residency.

Costs on top of the price
6-9% · The buyer pays an agent fee capped at 3% plus ¥60,000 plus 10% consumption tax (with a special cap of up to ¥330,000 including tax for cheap vacant homes up to ¥8 million), registration tax of 1.5% on land (until March 2029) and 2% standard on the building, real estate acquisition tax of 3% of assessed value, stamp duty, and a judicial scrivener fee of about ¥100,000 to ¥200,000.

Yearly property tax
Fixed asset tax is 1.4% of the government's assessed value, plus city planning tax of up to 0.3% in urban areas, and small residential plots get a lower tax base.

Tax on rental income
Rent paid to a non-resident is subject to 20.42% withholding (except when an individual rents it as their own home), and the owner must file a tax return each year through a tax representative in Japan to settle the final tax.

## Buying a home in Lombok: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Same Indonesian rules as Bali: no freehold; leasehold, Hak Pakai, or HGB via a PT PMA.

Costs on top of the price
6.5-18% · BPHTB 5% + notary 1-2.5% + legal 0.5-1.5%; +11% PPN/VAT on new developer units unless the 2026 VAT incentive applies.

Yearly property tax
PBB, up to ~0.5% of assessed (NJOP-based) value.

Tax on rental income
Non-residents: 20% withholding on gross rent (10% possible under a treaty); PT PMA 22% corporate tax.

What holiday rentals earn
No independent gross-yield figure found. Airbtics (Feb 2025-Jan 2026) South Lombok: 64% occupancy, ADR ~US$78, median revenue ~US$18k/yr, graded C+ and in the lowest 48% for STR yield in Southeast Asia. Developer projections (Lombok International Development) of 6.8-14.8% NET are not independent.

Holiday-rental rules
Pondok Wisata licence required for short-term rental; foreigners must operate through a PT PMA.

## Buying a home in Mexico: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes, but in the Restricted Zone (within 50 km of the coast or 100 km of borders, which covers Tulum and Playa del Carmen) only through a fideicomiso bank trust or a Mexican company; direct ownership elsewhere.

Costs on top of the price
3.5-8% · Acquisition tax 2-5% + notary 0.5-1% + legal 1-1.5% (GPG 3.5-7.5%), plus 0.5-1.5% for fideicomiso/permit setup; TheLatinvestor budgets 5-8%.

Yearly property tax
Municipal predial, set locally on cadastral value; usually small, often less than HOA fees.

Tax on rental income
Non-residents: 25% ISR withholding on gross rent; plus 16% IVA on short-term stays (Airbnb remits on its bookings).

What holiday rentals earn
No sourced STR gross yield. AirDNA (early 2026, via Virestia): Tulum average occupancy 44%, 8,000+ listings, bottom 80% of condos earn US$13-18k/yr at 31-44% occupancy. TheLatinvestor: Tulum ADR US$125, down 23% YoY.

Long-term rent yield
4.6-6.1 (GPG Q2 2026: Merida 6.08, Cancun 4.60, national 5.79)% gross

Holiday-rental rules
Quintana Roo: mandatory RETUR-Q registration (since Aug 2025, renewed annually) plus a state operating licence and RFC tax ID; 6% lodging tax; fines up to MXN 100,000.

## Buying a home in Montenegro: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes, houses and apartments freely; land requires a local company.

Costs on top of the price
1-4% · New build: 21% VAT is normally included in the developer price, buyer pays notary + ~1% legal; resale: 3% transfer tax (progressive on higher values) + notary + ~1% legal (GPG 4.01%).

Yearly property tax
Municipal, ~0.25-1% of assessed value (higher rates possible for tourist properties).

Tax on rental income
Around 15% withholding for non-residents.

What holiday rentals earn
No sourced STR gross yield found.

Long-term rent yield
4.4-5.2 (GPG Q2 2026: Podgorica 5.15, Budva 5.01, Tivat 4.36, national 4.84)% gross

Holiday-rental rules
Short-term rentals must be registered and pay a municipal tourist tax per guest-night.

## Buying a home in the Netherlands: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes. There are no nationality or residence rules and no surcharge for foreign buyers. Some cities, such as The Hague, restrict renting out cheaper homes after purchase without a permit (opkoopbescherming).

Costs on top of the price
2-9% · Transfer tax (overdrachtsbelasting) of 8% if you will not live in the home, such as a buy-to-let or holiday home, or 2% if it becomes your main home; a notary fee for the transfer deed of around EUR 500; Kadaster registration fees; and mortgage costs if you borrow; the seller pays its own agent.

Yearly property tax
Owners pay municipal property tax (onroerendezaakbelasting, OZB) on the official WOZ value, at a rate each municipality sets, which in practice is a per mille figure; tenants of homes do not pay it.

Tax on rental income
Non-residents declare Dutch property in box 3, where tax is 36% on a deemed return of 6% of the property's value in 2026, after a tax-free allowance of EUR 59,357 per person, regardless of actual rent.

## Buying a home in Northern Cyprus: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes, up to 3 properties (land cap ~1,338 m2), but each needs Council of Ministers Permission to Purchase (1-6 months); title-deed history risk.

Costs on top of the price
12-22% · Title deed transfer fee for foreigners 6-12% (sources disagree: 9% most cited, 12% in one 2026 guide) + 5% VAT on new builds (one source says 19%) + 0.5% stamp duty + legal GBP 1,000-2,500 + transformer fee GBP 1,500-3,000 on new builds.

Yearly property tax
Per m2, very low: about GBP 10-100/yr for a typical apartment or villa.

Tax on rental income
10% of gross rental income (Investra, 2026).

What holiday rentals earn
No sourced gross yield; data conflict. Airbtics Jan 2026 Iskele: 75% occupancy, ADR EUR 84, ~EUR 24k/yr, 'top 1%' for STR yield in Southern Europe. AirROI 2025-26 Kyrenia: 37.1% occupancy, ADR US$99, ~US$10k/yr.

Holiday-rental rules
Must register with the Ministry of Tourism and hold a licence for short-term letting; monthly tax reporting.

## Buying a home in Norway: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes. Anyone with the funds can buy property in Norway, and a built plot of up to 2 decares normally needs no concession (konsesjon) or self-declaration; owning property gives no right to live there.

Costs on top of the price
2.5-3% · Document duty (dokumentavgift) of 2.5% of market value, a registration fee (tinglysingsgebyr) of NOK 545 for the deed and NOK 545 for any mortgage document; a flat in a housing cooperative (borettslag) has no document duty; the seller normally pays the agent.

Yearly property tax
Some municipalities charge property tax (eiendomsskatt), at most 4 per mille of the value after a reduction of at least 30%, and some also give a basic deduction; many charge nothing.

Tax on rental income
Rental profit is normally taxed at 22%, and the Tax Administration says its rental rules also apply to owners who are tax resident abroad.

## Buying a home in Poland: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
EU, EEA and Swiss citizens buy on the same terms as Poles. Other foreigners can buy an apartment without a permit, but usually need a permit from the Ministry of the Interior (MSWiA) to buy a house or land.

Costs on top of the price
2.5-4% · Tax on civil law transactions (PCC) 2% of the value, paid by the buyer within 14 days of the deed; notary fee (taksa notarialna) capped at PLN 1,010 plus 0.4% of the value above PLN 60,000, plus 23% VAT; court fee of PLN 200 to enter ownership in the land register (plus PLN 100 for a new register); optional lawyer about 1%; the agent fee (about 2-3%) depends on the agreement.

Yearly property tax
Owners pay a local property tax (podatek od nieruchomości) set by the commune, capped in 2026 at PLN 1.25 per m² of usable floor space for flats and houses.

Tax on rental income
Private rental income is taxed as a flat lump sum (ryczałt) of 8.5% of revenue up to PLN 100,000 a year and 12.5% above that.

## Buying a home in Portugal: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes, same rights as Portuguese citizens (IMT increase for foreign second-home buyers announced Sept 2025).

Costs on top of the price
3-12% · IMT transfer tax 0-8% (progressive) + stamp duty 0.8% + notary/registry 0.9-1.2% + legal 1.25-2%.

Yearly property tax
IMI 0.3-0.45% of taxable value (urban), set by municipality.

Tax on rental income
Long-term: 25% flat for non-residents; short-term (AL) under the simplified regime only 35-50% of gross is taxable.

What holiday rentals earn
No sourced STR gross yield found.

Long-term rent yield
3.8-4.9 (GPG Q2 2026: national 4.29, Lisbon 3.76, Porto 3.96, Faro 4.48)% gross

Holiday-rental rules
Alojamento Local (AL) registration is mandatory; since Nov 2024 municipalities can freeze new AL licences in containment zones (Lisbon, Porto use this); condominiums can object with >50% of owners.

## Buying a home in Spain: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes, no restrictions at present; the government has proposed a 100% tax on (or ban for) non-EU non-resident buyers, not enacted.

Costs on top of the price
7.5-14% · New build: 10% IVA + 0.5-1.5% AJD stamp duty + notary 0.5-1% + legal 1-2%; resale: ITP transfer tax 6-11% instead of IVA/AJD.

Yearly property tax
IBI 0.4-1.1% of cadastral value (municipal), plus imputed income tax on unlet homes.

Tax on rental income
Non-residents: EU/EEA 19% on net income; non-EU 24% on gross with no deductions.

Holiday-rental yield
5-7% gross

What holiday rentals earn
Gross, Global Investments guide 2026 for Costa del Sol, Valencia, Canary Islands; realistic net 3-4.5% before tax. GPG long-term: national 5.51%, Alicante 6.80, Murcia 6.06, Malaga 4.97.

Long-term rent yield
4.7-6.8 (GPG Q3 2026, national 5.51)% gross

Holiday-rental rules
Regional tourist licence plus the national single rental registry number (mandatory since 1 Jul 2025); new tourist lets in apartment blocks need 3/5 owners' approval (since 3 Apr 2025).

## Buying a home in Sweden: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes. There are no citizenship or residence rules for buying a home in Sweden, but you need a Swedish personal identity number or coordination number (samordningsnummer) to register ownership.

Costs on top of the price
1.5-3.5% · Stamp duty on the title (lagfart) of 1.5% of the price or tax value, whichever is higher, plus a SEK 825 fee; if you borrow and need new mortgage deeds (pantbrev), 2% of their amount plus a SEK 375 fee; optional legal advice; the seller normally pays the agent, and a cooperative flat (bostadsrätt) has no lagfart.

Yearly property tax
Houses pay a municipal property fee (kommunal fastighetsavgift) of SEK 10,425 in 2026, or 0.75% of the tax value if that is lower.

Tax on rental income
Non-resident individuals pay 30% tax on net rental income as capital income; for a private home you can first deduct SEK 40,000 per property and 20% of the rent (the 20% does not apply to a bostadsrätt).

## Buying a home in Switzerland: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Under the Lex Koller law, EU/EFTA citizens living in Switzerland and holders of a C permit buy like Swiss citizens, and non-EU holders of a B permit can buy a home they live in. People living abroad need a cantonal permit and can usually only buy one holiday home in a tourist area, within national quotas; a proposed tightening was under consultation in 2026.

Costs on top of the price
1-5% · Transfer tax (Handänderungssteuer, droits de mutation) 0% to about 3.3% depending on the canton; notary about 0.1-0.5%; land register fee, a small fixed amount or percentage; optional lawyer 1-2%; the agent fee (2-3%) is paid by the seller.

Yearly property tax
More than half of the cantons charge an annual property tax (Liegenschaftssteuer), usually 0.01-0.3% of the assessed value, and owners also pay cantonal wealth tax on the property value minus the mortgage.

Tax on rental income
Non-residents pay tax on net Swiss rental income at ordinary cantonal and communal rates plus federal direct tax, and some cantons set the rate using worldwide income.

## Buying a home in the United Kingdom: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes. There are no nationality restrictions on buying homes anywhere in the UK and no visa is needed, but buying does not give a right to live there.

Costs on top of the price
3-9% · In England and Northern Ireland, Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) is 0% up to £125,000 and 2% from £125,001 to £250,000, plus a 2% surcharge for non-UK residents and a further 5% if you already own a home anywhere, so a non-resident who owns another home pays 7% up to £125,000 and 9% to £250,000; solicitor (conveyancer) about 0.6-1% with a typical minimum of around £2,100 including VAT; Land Registry fee £20 to £230; searches extra; the seller pays the estate agent.

Yearly property tax
Owners or occupiers pay council tax to the local council, and many councils in England charge second homes a premium of up to 100% from April 2025.

Tax on rental income
Non-resident landlords pay UK income tax on rent at 20%, 40% or 45%, with 20% deducted at source by the agent or tenant unless HMRC approves gross payment, and the rates on property income are set to rise to 22%, 42% and 47% from April 2027.

## Buying a home in the United States: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Yes. There is no federal ban on foreigners buying homes, but about 30 states have added some limits, and Texas and Florida restrict buyers from certain countries such as China.

Costs on top of the price
2-5% · Closing costs vary by state and typically run 2-5% of the loan amount, covering title search and title insurance, recording fees, attorney fees, appraisal and lender fees; since August 2024 the seller no longer has to pay the buyer's agent, so the buyer may pay it unless the seller agrees to; FIRPTA does not apply when you buy but does when a foreigner later sells, with the buyer generally withholding 15% of the sale price.

Yearly property tax
Property tax is set locally and in 2024 averaged about 1.22% of value across the largest city in each state, from 0.30% in Honolulu to 3.02% in Detroit.

Tax on rental income
By default a non-resident pays 30% of gross rent (or a lower treaty rate), withheld at source, or can elect to treat the rent as business income and pay graduated rates on net income by filing Form 1040-NR and giving Form W-8ECI to the withholding agent.

## Buying a home in Vietnam: what it really costs

Can foreigners buy?
Only buildings (mostly condos) on a 50-year renewable term, never land; caps of 30% of units per apartment building and 250 houses per ward.

Costs on top of the price
2.5-3.1% · New developer apartment: 10% VAT usually already in the price + 0.5% registration fee + 2% maintenance fund + notary/admin; GPG lists 2.55-3.1% buyer costs.

Yearly property tax
Non-agricultural land-use tax 0.03-0.15% of state land value; negligible for apartments.

Tax on rental income
10% of gross rent (5% VAT + 5% PIT) above the exemption threshold; threshold raised to VND 1 billion/yr from 1 Jan 2026 (older guides say VND 100 million).

What holiday rentals earn
No sourced STR gross yield found.

Long-term rent yield
3.5-4.2 (GPG Q3 2025: HCMC 4.16, Hanoi 3.54)% gross

Holiday-rental rules
Guests must be registered with local police; HCMC (Decision 19/2026, from 25 Apr 2026) allows apartment short-lets only as registered, licensed accommodation providers; frequent/multi-unit renting needs a business registration.

## How to buy a home in Bulgaria as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes, buildings and apartments, with rights similar to locals; per GPG, foreigners can't own land directly, so a Bulgarian company is the usual route.

### The steps

- Check what you can own: Non-EU citizens can buy apartments and buildings in their own name but not land. To buy a house with its plot, a non-EU buyer usually sets up a Bulgarian company.
- Hire a lawyer and check the property: A lawyer checks the title and debts, which usually takes 5 to 10 business days.
- Sign a preliminary contract: Pay a deposit, usually 10%. If you pull out you lose it, and if the seller pulls out they owe you double.
- Get your documents ready: You need your passport and a Bulgarian personal tax number from the National Revenue Agency. Payments of EUR 5,113 or more must go by bank transfer.
- Sign the deed before a notary: Sign the notarial deed before a notary in the property's district, with a sworn translator if you do not speak Bulgarian. The notary files it with the Registry Agency, usually in 1 to 3 business days.
- Declare the property to the municipality: File a tax declaration with the local municipality within 2 months of buying, and move the utility accounts into your name.

### Costs on top of the price

About 3.2-8.5%: Transfer tax 0.1-3% (municipal; Sofia 2.5%) + notary 0.1-1.5% + legal 0.5-1% + agent 2.5-3%.

### Every year

Yearly costs are low: municipal property tax is 0.01% to 0.45% of the tax assessment value, with a 5% discount if paid in full by April 30, plus a municipal waste collection fee. Owning through a company adds about EUR 500 to 1,500 a year in running costs.

Yearly property tax: 0.01-0.45% of the property's tax value plus a municipal garbage fee.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents: 10% final tax on gross rent, paid quarterly, no deductions.

## How to buy a home in Canada as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Mostly not for now: a federal ban stops non-Canadians from buying homes in cities and larger towns until January 1, 2027, with exceptions such as work permit holders and spouses of citizens or permanent residents. The ban does not cover rural areas and small towns, and the government has said it does not plan simply to extend it, but a replacement is being studied.

### The steps

- Check if you can buy: Until January 1, 2027, non-Canadians cannot buy homes in census metropolitan areas or census agglomerations unless an exception applies. Check the location and your status first.
- Check provincial foreign buyer taxes: Ontario charges foreign buyers 25% and British Columbia charges 20% in some regions. These taxes can cost more than the rest of the purchase costs combined.
- Hire a real estate lawyer: The lawyer checks the title, handles the funds and registers the transfer. Ask for a written fee estimate first.
- Make an offer: Sign a purchase agreement with your price and conditions, such as a home inspection.
- Close the sale: On closing day you pay the balance plus land transfer tax and fees through your lawyer, and the home is registered in your name.
- Arrange rental tax filings: If you rent it out, name a Canadian agent to withhold tax, consider filing Form NR6, and file a Section 216 return each year.

### Costs on top of the price

About 1.5-4%: Buyers usually pay provincial land transfer tax on a sliding scale (Ontario: 0.5% up to $55,000 and 1% from $55,000 to $250,000), legal fees of about $500 to $1,500, title insurance of about $250 and an inspection of $300 to $1,000, while the seller usually pays the agents; foreign buyers also pay Ontario's 25% non-resident speculation tax anywhere in Ontario and British Columbia's 20% additional tax in Metro Vancouver and four other regions.

### Every year

Expect municipal property tax, from about 0.3% to 2.1% of assessed value depending on the city, plus insurance and upkeep. The federal Underused Housing Tax is proposed to end from 2025, but the change was still in Bill C-15 when last checked.

Yearly property tax: Property tax is set by each city as a share of assessed value, from about 0.3% in Vancouver to 2.12% in Saint John in 2026.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents have 25% of gross rent withheld, but they can file a Section 216 return to pay tax on net rent instead, and Form NR6 lets the agent withhold on net rent.

## How to buy a home in Cyprus as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

EU citizens buy without restrictions. Non-EU buyers need permission from the Council of Ministers, applied for through the District Officer, and are normally limited to one home or a plot of up to 4,014 m².

### The steps

- Hire a lawyer: Use a Cyprus lawyer to negotiate and draft the sale contract and run the checks.
- Check the title: The lawyer searches the District Land Registry for ownership, mortgages, court claims and restrictions, and checks permits and VAT status.
- Sign the contract: Sign the sale agreement with the price and payment terms. It is legally binding once signed.
- Lodge the contract: Deposit the signed contract at the Land Registry under the Specific Performance Law to protect your right to the title.
- Apply for permission if non-EU: Non-EU buyers apply to the Council of Ministers through the District Officer, usually after signing. The title cannot be registered without it.
- Transfer the title: Pay the balance and transfer fees, then transfer the title deed at the District Land Registry.

### Costs on top of the price

About 2.5-3.5%: Land Registry transfer fees of 3% up to €85,000, 5% to €170,000 and 8% above, halved for resales without VAT (1.5%, 2.5% and 4%); stamp duty abolished from 1 January 2026; lawyer about 1% plus VAT; small Land Registry charges.

### Every year

Yearly costs are municipal, sewerage and local authority fees, plus income tax and GHS on any rent.

Yearly property tax: There is no annual national property tax (abolished in 2017); owners pay municipal fees of about €90 to €300 a year, plus sewerage and local authority charges.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents pay income tax on Cyprus rental income at 20% to 35% after deducting 20% of the gross rent and loan interest, plus a 2.65% health contribution (GHS); the special defence contribution does not apply to them.

## How to buy a home in Denmark as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Without Danish domicile or 5 years of past residence you need permission from the Department of Civil Affairs (Civilstyrelsen); EU/EEA citizens who live and are registered in Denmark can buy a permanent home without permission by signing a declaration to the Land Registration Court. Holiday homes (sommerhuse) need permission, which is only given to people with particularly strong ties to Denmark, such as many years of holidays there.

### The steps

- Check if you need permission: Use Civilstyrelsen's rules: EU/EEA citizens living in Denmark sign a declaration, everyone else applies for permission for the specific property.
- Get a Danish tax number: If you have no Danish personal number, request one from the Danish Tax Agency with form 04.063_AP_EN.
- Set a budget with a bank: Danish banks usually lend up to 80% of the value, so plan for at least a 20% down payment.
- Make an offer and sign with conditions: The seller's agent drafts the contract; have your own lawyer review it and add bank and lawyer approval clauses (bank- og advokatforbehold).
- Let your lawyer check the documents: Your lawyer reviews the condition report, title and registered charges before the clauses are lifted.
- Register the deed: The deed (skøde) is registered digitally with the Land Registration Court and the registration fee is paid, which makes you the legal owner.

### Costs on top of the price

About 1.5-3%: Registration fee on the deed (tinglysningsafgift) of DKK 1,850 plus 0.6% of the price, about 1% for a buyer's lawyer, and, if you borrow, a mortgage registration fee of DKK 1,825 plus 1.25% of the loan; the seller normally pays the agent.

### Every year

Expect property value tax and municipal land tax, both charged through the Danish tax system, plus insurance, utilities and upkeep. Owners abroad may need to file a Danish tax return if they rent the home out.

Yearly property tax: Owners pay property value tax (ejendomsværdiskat) of 0.51% on 80% of the official valuation (1.4% above DKK 9.2 million) plus municipal land tax (grundskyld) at a rate set by each municipality, capped at 30 per mille of the land value.

Tax on rental income: A non-resident who rents out a Danish home is taxed in Denmark on the profit under the ordinary Danish rules; staying in Denmark more than 3 months at a time or 180 days a year, or working there, makes you fully tax liable.

## How to buy a home in the Dominican Republic as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes. Foreigners have the same rights as Dominican citizens to buy land and homes, with no restrictions.

### The steps

- Get a tax ID (RNC): Get your RNC at a DGII office with your passport, or through a lawyer with a notarized power of attorney. You need it to sign and to register the title.
- Check the title: Have a Dominican lawyer confirm a clean title at the Title Registry, with no liens or lawsuits, and that IPI tax, utilities and condo fees are paid.
- Sign a promise of sale: Sign the promise of sale contract and pay a deposit, usually 10-20%. It usually sets a 30 to 60 day window to complete.
- Sign the deed before a notary: Pay the balance and sign the deed of sale. The notary legalizes the document.
- Pay the transfer tax: Pay the 3% transfer tax to DGII. The title cannot be registered until it is paid.
- Register the title: Your lawyer files the deed and tax receipt at the Title Registry. The new title certificate in your name usually takes 30 to 90 days.

### Costs on top of the price

About 4.25-7%: The buyer pays a 3% transfer tax (0% for qualifying first purchases under CONFOTUR tourism incentives), legal fees of about 1-2% and notary fees of about 0.25-1%, plus registration costs, while the seller pays the 2-3% agent fee.

### Every year

Most single homes under about $150,000 pay no IPI property tax because they fall under the threshold, but expect condo fees, utilities and upkeep. A 2026 tax law (Law 30-26) sets a 10% tax on gains when an individual sells, though its regulations were still in draft in October 2026.

Yearly property tax: The yearly IPI tax is 1% of the part of a person's total Dominican property value, as assessed by the tax office DGII, above RD$10,695,494 in 2026, so a single cheap home is often below the threshold.

Tax on rental income: Rent paid abroad to a non-resident is generally subject to 27% withholding.

## How to buy a home in France as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes. Foreigners can buy property in France without major restrictions, and non-EU buyers do not need a permit, although the paperwork can take longer.

### The steps

- Make an offer: Agree the price with the seller, usually through the agent. Budget for notary fees and other costs first.
- Sign the preliminary contract: Sign the compromis de vente with a notary (notaire). Add conditions (clauses suspensives) such as getting a mortgage.
- Use the cooling-off period: You have 10 days after receiving the signed compromis to withdraw without penalty. The seller cannot withdraw.
- Pay the deposit: After the cooling-off period, pay a deposit, usually 10% of the price. You may lose it if you pull out without a valid condition.
- Let the notary run checks: The notary checks ownership, boundaries and rights of way and collects the compulsory diagnostic surveys (termites, lead, asbestos).
- Sign the final deed: Send the balance and fees to the notary's account before the date, then sign the acte de vente in person or by power of attorney. The notary registers the sale.

### Costs on top of the price

About 7-8.5%: Transfer taxes (droits de mutation) of about 5.8%, or about 6.3% in departments that raised their rate for 2025 to March 2028; notary fee (émoluments) on a sliding scale from 3.87% down to 0.799% plus 20% VAT, about 1.3% on a €150,000 home; land security contribution (contribution de sécurité immobilière) 0.10%; disbursements (débours) of about €800 to €1,200; the agent fee is usually built into the advertised price (FAI) and paid by the seller, sometimes shared.

### Every year

Expect the annual taxe foncière, plus taxe d'habitation if the home is a furnished second home, and income tax and social charges on any rent.

Yearly property tax: Owners pay an annual property tax (taxe foncière) set by the local authorities, and owners of a furnished second home also pay housing tax (taxe d'habitation), which some communes raise by a surcharge of 5% to 60%.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents pay French income tax on French rental income at a minimum rate of 20% (30% above about €27,500), plus social charges of 17.2%, or 7.5% for people covered by social security in another EU/EEA country or Switzerland.

## How to buy a home in Germany as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes. There are no restrictions on foreigners buying property in Germany, though non-EU buyers usually need a bigger down payment to get a loan.

### The steps

- Find a home and arrange money: Search the portals or use a local agent and get financing in place before signing.
- Get independent advice: The notary is neutral and does not act for you, so consider your own lawyer and a survey.
- Sign before a notary: The notary drafts the purchase contract and both sides sign it in front of the notary; you can sign through a certified power of attorney from abroad.
- Secure a priority notice: The notary registers a priority notice (Vormerkung) in the land register to protect you against other sales.
- Pay the transfer tax and the price: Pay the transfer tax when the tax office sends the bill, and pay the price as the contract sets out, often via the notary.
- Get registered as owner: The land registry (Grundbuch) enters you as owner once the transfer tax is paid, which can take 3 to 4 months.

### Costs on top of the price

About 5-8.5%: Real estate transfer tax (Grunderwerbsteuer) of 3.5% to 6.5% depending on the state (3.5% in Bavaria, 6.5% in Brandenburg, North Rhine-Westphalia, Saarland and Schleswig-Holstein), plus notary and land registry fees (Notar- und Grundbuchkosten) of about 1.5-2%; if the seller hired the agent, the buyer pays half the commission by law, which is extra.

### Every year

Expect the municipal property tax, insurance, utilities and upkeep. Rental profit is taxable in Germany, so a non-resident landlord deals with a German tax office.

Yearly property tax: Owners pay property tax (Grundsteuer), calculated since 2025 as assessed value x a tax rate x a municipal multiplier (Hebesatz) that each municipality sets.

Tax on rental income: Non-resident owners are taxed in Germany on net rental income at the normal progressive income tax rates, but without the basic tax-free allowance (Grundfreibetrag).

## How to buy a home in Greece as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes. Buyers from outside the EU and EFTA need a permit to buy in designated border areas (parts of northern Greece and eastern Aegean islands such as the Dodecanese and Rhodes). The government has announced a 15% transfer tax for non-EU buyers of homes from 1 January 2027, not yet final in September 2026.

### The steps

- Get a Greek tax number: Apply for a tax number (AFM) with your passport. It is free and needed to sign contracts and pay taxes.
- Hire a lawyer: A lawyer is not mandatory but is strongly recommended. They can act for you under a power of attorney.
- Check the title: The lawyer checks ownership and searches the land registry for mortgages, liens and claims. Non-EU buyers in border areas apply for the permit at this stage.
- Sign a private agreement: Sign a preliminary purchase agreement and pay a deposit, usually 5-10%, which you normally lose if you withdraw.
- Pay the transfer tax: The notary prepares the transfer tax declaration and you pay the tax before the final deed.
- Sign the deed and register it: Sign the final contract before a notary and pay the balance, usually on the same day. The deed is then registered at the local land registry or cadastre.

### Costs on top of the price

About 5.5-7%: Transfer tax 3.09% of the price or the taxable value, whichever is higher; notary about 0.8-1% plus VAT; land registry fees about 0.5-0.7%; lawyer 1-2% plus VAT; if an agent is used, the buyer usually pays a commission of 1-3% plus VAT on top.

### Every year

Yearly costs are ENFIA and income tax on any rent.

Yearly property tax: Owners on 1 January pay the unified property tax (ENFIA), calculated per property from its location, size, age and official zone value, with an extra charge if total Greek property exceeds €500,000.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents pay Greek tax on Greek rental income at 15% up to €12,000, 25% to €24,000, 35% to €36,000 and 45% above, after a flat 5% deduction for expenses.

## How to buy a home in Italy as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes for EU citizens; non-EU buyers need reciprocity (US, UK, Canada, Australia qualify).

### The steps

- Get a codice fiscale: Your Italian tax code. It is free, from the Agenzia delle Entrate in Italy or an Italian consulate abroad.
- Make a written offer: The proposta d'acquisto usually comes with a small deposit. Once accepted, many buyers sign a preliminary contract (compromesso) with a 10–30% deposit.
- Check the house: Ask for the land registry extract (visura catastale), proof the building matches its plans (conformità urbanistica e catastale), the energy certificate (APE) and any unpaid debts on the property.
- Sign at the notary: The deed (rogito) is signed before a notaio, who checks the title and registers the sale. You can sign by power of attorney if you cannot travel.
- Pay the taxes: Buying from a private seller: registration tax 9% of the cadastral value for a second home, or 2% if it becomes your main home, plus €50 + €50 fixed taxes and the notary's fee.

### Costs on top of the price

About 4-15%: Registration tax 9% on a second home (resale), or VAT on new builds; notary 1-2% + legal ~1% + agent ~3% (GPG roundtrip 10-18%).

### Every year

IMU (council property tax) on second homes and a local waste tax (TARI). For small rural houses these are often a few hundred euros a year.

Yearly property tax: IMU 0.4-1.06% on second homes (on cadastral value).

Tax on rental income: Optional flat 'cedolare secca' on short lets: 21% for one property, 26% from the second.

## How to buy a home in Japan as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes. Foreigners can buy freehold land and homes on the same terms as Japanese citizens, even on a tourist visa, though buying does not give a visa or residency.

### The steps

- Find a home and agent: Any licensed agent can show you most listings. Many cheap homes are only advertised in Japanese, so an agent who translates helps.
- Submit a written offer: Send a non-binding purchase application with your price and conditions. Non-residents usually pay cash, since Japanese banks rarely lend to them.
- Hear the property explanation: Before the contract, a licensed specialist must explain the property's legal status. This can be done by video call.
- Sign and pay a deposit: Sign the sale contract and pay a deposit of about 5-10%. If you pull out after this, you lose the deposit.
- Pay and register: On settlement day you pay the balance and get the keys, and a judicial scrivener registers the transfer at the Legal Affairs Bureau. Since October 5, 2026 all buyers must show proof of nationality when registering.
- File reports and name a tax representative: Non-residents must report the purchase to the Bank of Japan within 20 days under the Foreign Exchange Act. You also need a tax representative with a Japanese address to receive and pay tax bills.

### Costs on top of the price

About 6-9%: The buyer pays an agent fee capped at 3% plus ¥60,000 plus 10% consumption tax (with a special cap of up to ¥330,000 including tax for cheap vacant homes up to ¥8 million), registration tax of 1.5% on land (until March 2029) and 2% standard on the building, real estate acquisition tax of 3% of assessed value, stamp duty, and a judicial scrivener fee of about ¥100,000 to ¥200,000.

### Every year

Expect fixed asset tax of 1.4% and city planning tax of up to 0.3% of assessed value, which is usually well below market value. Add the cost of a tax representative and, for apartments, monthly management and repair fund fees.

Yearly property tax: Fixed asset tax is 1.4% of the government's assessed value, plus city planning tax of up to 0.3% in urban areas, and small residential plots get a lower tax base.

Tax on rental income: Rent paid to a non-resident is subject to 20.42% withholding (except when an individual rents it as their own home), and the owner must file a tax return each year through a tax representative in Japan to settle the final tax.

## How to buy a home in Mexico as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes, but in the Restricted Zone (within 50 km of the coast or 100 km of borders, which covers Tulum and Playa del Carmen) only through a fideicomiso bank trust or a Mexican company; direct ownership elsewhere.

### The steps

- Check the restricted zone: Foreigners cannot hold title directly within 50 km of the coast or 100 km of a border. Outside that zone you can own in your own name.
- Choose how to hold title: In the restricted zone use a bank trust (fideicomiso), where a Mexican bank holds title for you, or a Mexican company. The foreign ministry (SRE) permit cost MXN 21,650 for a trust in 2026.
- Check the title: Verify the seller's title, check for liens and disputes, and confirm the land is not ejido land, which cannot be sold normally.
- Sign the purchase contract: Sign a contract that sets the price, payment terms and conditions. Do not wire a deposit until the documents and title have been reviewed.
- Close with a notary: A public notary prepares and signs the public deed (escritura). A separate buyer's lawyer is recommended for an independent review.
- Register the deed: The notary registers the deed in the Public Registry. Keep the final escritura and registration records.

### Costs on top of the price

About 3.5-8%: Acquisition tax 2-5% + notary 0.5-1% + legal 1-1.5% (GPG 3.5-7.5%), plus 0.5-1.5% for fideicomiso/permit setup; TheLatinvestor budgets 5-8%.

### Every year

Yearly costs include the local property tax (predial), usually 0.05% to 1.2% of the official cadastral value, which is often well below market value. In the restricted zone add the bank trust fee, about US$450 to US$1,000 a year, plus HOA fees, insurance and upkeep.

Yearly property tax: Municipal predial, set locally on cadastral value; usually small, often less than HOA fees.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents: 25% ISR withholding on gross rent; plus 16% IVA on short-term stays (Airbnb remits on its bookings).

## How to buy a home in the Netherlands as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes. There are no nationality or residence rules and no surcharge for foreign buyers. Some cities, such as The Hague, restrict renting out cheaper homes after purchase without a permit (opkoopbescherming).

### The steps

- Get a BSN: Register in person at one of the 19 RNI municipalities with a valid ID to get a citizen service number (BSN).
- Set up payment and money: Open an account that can pay the notary on time and arrange financing.
- Make an offer: A verbal or email acceptance does not bind you; only a signed written purchase agreement (koopovereenkomst) does.
- Use the 3-day cooling-off period: A private buyer can cancel within three days of receiving the signed agreement without giving a reason.
- Pay the deposit: The standard agreement usually asks for 10% of the price, or a bank guarantee, paid to the notary.
- Sign the deed and register: A Dutch civil-law notary signs the transfer deed and you become owner when it is registered with the Kadaster.

### Costs on top of the price

About 2-9%: Transfer tax (overdrachtsbelasting) of 8% if you will not live in the home, such as a buy-to-let or holiday home, or 2% if it becomes your main home; a notary fee for the transfer deed of around EUR 500; Kadaster registration fees; and mortgage costs if you borrow; the seller pays its own agent.

### Every year

Expect municipal property tax (OZB), insurance and upkeep, and in a flat the owners' association (VvE) contribution. Non-residents also pay box 3 income tax based on the property's value.

Yearly property tax: Owners pay municipal property tax (onroerendezaakbelasting, OZB) on the official WOZ value, at a rate each municipality sets, which in practice is a per mille figure; tenants of homes do not pay it.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents declare Dutch property in box 3, where tax is 36% on a deemed return of 6% of the property's value in 2026, after a tax-free allowance of EUR 59,357 per person, regardless of actual rent.

## How to buy a home in Norway as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes. Anyone with the funds can buy property in Norway, and a built plot of up to 2 decares normally needs no concession (konsesjon) or self-declaration; owning property gives no right to live there.

### The steps

- Find a home and get loan approval: Search listings on Finn.no and get pre-approval if you need a mortgage; expect to put down 15 to 25%.
- Bid through the agent: Offers go through the seller's agent and bidding rounds can close within 24 hours, so inspect the home first.
- Sign the contract: The agent draws up the purchase contract; have a local lawyer review it.
- Pay at settlement: The price is paid through an escrow account at closing, and the deed is signed.
- Get a D-number if needed: Send Kartverket's D-number application with the deed and a certified passport copy no more than 3 months old.
- Register the deed: The deed (skjøte) is registered with Kartverket and the 2.5% document duty and fee are paid.

### Costs on top of the price

About 2.5-3%: Document duty (dokumentavgift) of 2.5% of market value, a registration fee (tinglysingsgebyr) of NOK 545 for the deed and NOK 545 for any mortgage document; a flat in a housing cooperative (borettslag) has no document duty; the seller normally pays the agent.

### Every year

Expect municipal property tax where it applies, municipal fees, insurance and upkeep. Costs such as municipal fees and property tax are deductible against rental income.

Yearly property tax: Some municipalities charge property tax (eiendomsskatt), at most 4 per mille of the value after a reduction of at least 30%, and some also give a basic deduction; many charge nothing.

Tax on rental income: Rental profit is normally taxed at 22%, and the Tax Administration says its rental rules also apply to owners who are tax resident abroad.

## How to buy a home in Poland as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

EU, EEA and Swiss citizens buy on the same terms as Poles. Other foreigners can buy an apartment without a permit, but usually need a permit from the Ministry of the Interior (MSWiA) to buy a house or land.

### The steps

- Get a PESEL number: Apply for a Polish identification number (PESEL) in Poland, in person or through a lawyer with power of attorney. It is free and usually takes up to seven business days.
- Check if you need a permit: Non-EEA buyers of a house or land should apply for an MSWiA permit before buying. Apartments do not need one.
- Sign a preliminary agreement: Agree the price and pay a deposit, usually 10%. If you withdraw without cause the seller keeps it; if the seller withdraws they repay double.
- Do due diligence: A bilingual lawyer can check the land register (księga wieczysta) for liens, debts, unpaid fees and zoning issues.
- Sign the notarial deed: Sign the final deed (akt notarialny) before a notary and pay the fees. The notary files the change with the land register.
- Pay the PCC tax: Pay the 2% PCC within 14 days of the deed if the notary has not collected it.

### Costs on top of the price

About 2.5-4%: Tax on civil law transactions (PCC) 2% of the value, paid by the buyer within 14 days of the deed; notary fee (taksa notarialna) capped at PLN 1,010 plus 0.4% of the value above PLN 60,000, plus 23% VAT; court fee of PLN 200 to enter ownership in the land register (plus PLN 100 for a new register); optional lawyer about 1%; the agent fee (about 2-3%) depends on the agreement.

### Every year

Yearly costs are the local property tax, which is low for flats, plus income tax on any rent.

Yearly property tax: Owners pay a local property tax (podatek od nieruchomości) set by the commune, capped in 2026 at PLN 1.25 per m² of usable floor space for flats and houses.

Tax on rental income: Private rental income is taxed as a flat lump sum (ryczałt) of 8.5% of revenue up to PLN 100,000 a year and 12.5% above that.

## How to buy a home in Portugal as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes, same rights as Portuguese citizens (IMT increase for foreign second-home buyers announced Sept 2025).

### The steps

- Get a NIF: Your tax number, at a Finanças office or through a representative. Non-EU residents usually need a fiscal representative.
- Sign a promissory contract: The CPCV fixes price and date, with a deposit of 10–30%.
- Check the house: Ask for the caderneta predial and the certidão permanente (owner, debts, urban or rustic), and the habitation licence (licença de utilização).
- Sign the deed: At a notary or a Casa Pronta office, then the sale is registered at the Conservatória.
- Pay the taxes: IMT on a sliding scale up to about 8% (5% on rustic land) and stamp duty of 0.8%.

### Costs on top of the price

About 3-12%: IMT transfer tax 0-8% (progressive) + stamp duty 0.8% + notary/registry 0.9-1.2% + legal 1.25-2%.

### Every year

IMI (council tax), usually 0.3–0.45% of the tax value for urban property.

Yearly property tax: IMI 0.3-0.45% of taxable value (urban), set by municipality.

Tax on rental income: Long-term: 25% flat for non-residents; short-term (AL) under the simplified regime only 35-50% of gross is taxable.

## How to buy a home in Spain as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes, no restrictions at present; the government has proposed a 100% tax on (or ban for) non-EU non-resident buyers, not enacted.

### The steps

- Get an NIE: Your foreigner identity number, from a Spanish consulate or a police station in Spain. You need it to sign and to pay taxes.
- Open a Spanish bank account: Most notaries and councils expect payments and bills to go through a Spanish account.
- Reserve with an arras contract: A private contract with a deposit, usually 10%. If the seller backs out, they normally return it twice.
- Check the house: Order a nota simple from the Land Registry (owner and debts). In the countryside, check the land status (suelo rústico) and that the buildings are legal. Ask for the last IBI receipts.
- Sign at the notary and register: The escritura is signed before a notario and then registered at the Registro de la Propiedad.
- Pay the transfer tax: Resale homes pay ITP of 6–10% depending on the region, plus notary and registry of roughly €1,000–2,000.

### Costs on top of the price

About 7.5-14%: New build: 10% IVA + 0.5-1.5% AJD stamp duty + notary 0.5-1% + legal 1-2%; resale: ITP transfer tax 6-11% instead of IVA/AJD.

### Every year

IBI (council tax) and waste collection. Non-residents who do not rent the house out also file a small yearly imputed-income tax.

Yearly property tax: IBI 0.4-1.1% of cadastral value (municipal), plus imputed income tax on unlet homes.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents: EU/EEA 19% on net income; non-EU 24% on gross with no deductions.

## How to buy a home in Sweden as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes. There are no citizenship or residence rules for buying a home in Sweden, but you need a Swedish personal identity number or coordination number (samordningsnummer) to register ownership.

### The steps

- Get a coordination number: Book an identity check at a Swedish Tax Agency service centre to get a samordningsnummer, which you need to register as owner.
- Open a Swedish bank account: A Swedish account is normally needed to complete the payment.
- Find a home and arrange money: Listings are on Hemnet and Booli; foreign buyers may face a larger deposit if a bank lends at all.
- Inspect before you commit: Visit the property and consider hiring an inspector before signing.
- Sign the purchase contract: You and the seller sign the contract, usually with the seller's agent handling the paperwork.
- Apply for title at Lantmäteriet: Apply to Lantmäteriet for lagfart and pay the 1.5% stamp duty to be registered as owner.

### Costs on top of the price

About 1.5-3.5%: Stamp duty on the title (lagfart) of 1.5% of the price or tax value, whichever is higher, plus a SEK 825 fee; if you borrow and need new mortgage deeds (pantbrev), 2% of their amount plus a SEK 375 fee; optional legal advice; the seller normally pays the agent, and a cooperative flat (bostadsrätt) has no lagfart.

### Every year

House owners pay the municipal property fee and must file a Swedish tax return if they owe it or have rental income, even when living abroad. Add insurance, utilities and upkeep.

Yearly property tax: Houses pay a municipal property fee (kommunal fastighetsavgift) of SEK 10,425 in 2026, or 0.75% of the tax value if that is lower.

Tax on rental income: Non-resident individuals pay 30% tax on net rental income as capital income; for a private home you can first deduct SEK 40,000 per property and 20% of the rent (the 20% does not apply to a bostadsrätt).

## How to buy a home in Switzerland as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Under the Lex Koller law, EU/EFTA citizens living in Switzerland and holders of a C permit buy like Swiss citizens, and non-EU holders of a B permit can buy a home they live in. People living abroad need a cantonal permit and can usually only buy one holiday home in a tourist area, within national quotas; a proposed tightening was under consultation in 2026.

### The steps

- Check your Lex Koller status: Find out whether you can buy freely or need a permit. People living abroad must get authorisation from the canton before buying.
- Arrange financing: Banks usually require at least 20% of the price as equity and test affordability at an interest rate of about 5%.
- Find a property and make an offer: Search the main portals and make your offer, usually through the seller's agent.
- Sign the deed at a notary: The notary drafts the purchase contract (Kaufvertrag, acte de vente), reads it aloud and both parties sign it.
- Register the transfer: The notary files the sale with the land register (Grundbuch, registre foncier). Ownership passes once it is registered, which can take several weeks.

### Costs on top of the price

About 1-5%: Transfer tax (Handänderungssteuer, droits de mutation) 0% to about 3.3% depending on the canton; notary about 0.1-0.5%; land register fee, a small fixed amount or percentage; optional lawyer 1-2%; the agent fee (2-3%) is paid by the seller.

### Every year

Yearly costs are wealth tax, cantonal property tax where it exists, and tax on imputed rental value (Eigenmietwert) if you use the home yourself. Imputed rental value is due to end on 1 January 2029, and cantons may then add a new tax on second homes.

Yearly property tax: More than half of the cantons charge an annual property tax (Liegenschaftssteuer), usually 0.01-0.3% of the assessed value, and owners also pay cantonal wealth tax on the property value minus the mortgage.

Tax on rental income: Non-residents pay tax on net Swiss rental income at ordinary cantonal and communal rates plus federal direct tax, and some cantons set the rate using worldwide income.

## How to buy a home in the United Kingdom as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes. There are no nationality restrictions on buying homes anywhere in the UK and no visa is needed, but buying does not give a right to live there.

### The steps

- Make an offer: Make an offer through the seller's estate agent. Acceptance is not binding until contracts are exchanged.
- Instruct a solicitor: Hire a solicitor or licensed conveyancer. The whole process can be done remotely.
- Run searches and enquiries: Your solicitor runs local searches and raises questions with the seller. This stage often takes 8 to 12 weeks.
- Exchange contracts: Sign and exchange contracts and pay the deposit, usually 10%. You are now legally bound to buy.
- Complete: Pay the balance on the completion date and get the keys.
- Pay SDLT and register: Your solicitor pays the SDLT, files the return with HMRC and registers you as owner at HM Land Registry.

### Costs on top of the price

About 3-9%: In England and Northern Ireland, Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) is 0% up to £125,000 and 2% from £125,001 to £250,000, plus a 2% surcharge for non-UK residents and a further 5% if you already own a home anywhere, so a non-resident who owns another home pays 7% up to £125,000 and 9% to £250,000; solicitor (conveyancer) about 0.6-1% with a typical minimum of around £2,100 including VAT; Land Registry fee £20 to £230; searches extra; the seller pays the estate agent.

### Every year

Yearly costs are council tax, which may include a second home premium, plus a self assessment tax return and income tax if you let the home.

Yearly property tax: Owners or occupiers pay council tax to the local council, and many councils in England charge second homes a premium of up to 100% from April 2025.

Tax on rental income: Non-resident landlords pay UK income tax on rent at 20%, 40% or 45%, with 20% deducted at source by the agent or tenant unless HMRC approves gross payment, and the rates on property income are set to rise to 22%, 42% and 47% from April 2027.

## How to buy a home in the United States as a foreigner

The steps, papers and taxes, in plain words. General information, not legal advice: use a local lawyer before you sign.

### Can foreigners buy?

Yes. There is no federal ban on foreigners buying homes, but about 30 states have added some limits, and Texas and Florida restrict buyers from certain countries such as China.

### The steps

- Check the state rules: Confirm the state you are buying in does not restrict buyers from your country. Rules differ by state and some only cover farmland or land near military bases.
- Sign up with a buyer's agent: Agents must now have a written agreement with you before showing homes. It sets out how much the agent is paid and who pays it.
- Make an offer: Put your price and conditions in a written offer. You can ask the seller to pay all or part of your agent's commission.
- Do the checks: Get a home inspection and a title search so you know the condition of the house and that the title is clean.
- Close and record the deed: Pay the balance and closing costs at closing. The deed is then recorded with the county.
- Set up your tax filing: If you rent the home out, decide between 30% tax on gross rent or the net-income election, which needs Form W-8ECI and a yearly Form 1040-NR.

### Costs on top of the price

About 2-5%: Closing costs vary by state and typically run 2-5% of the loan amount, covering title search and title insurance, recording fees, attorney fees, appraisal and lender fees; since August 2024 the seller no longer has to pay the buyer's agent, so the buyer may pay it unless the seller agrees to; FIRPTA does not apply when you buy but does when a foreigner later sells, with the buyer generally withholding 15% of the sale price.

### Every year

Expect local property tax, which is often around 1% of value but varies widely by city, plus insurance and upkeep. If you rent it out you also file a US tax return each year when you use the net-income election.

Yearly property tax: Property tax is set locally and in 2024 averaged about 1.22% of value across the largest city in each state, from 0.30% in Honolulu to 3.02% in Detroit.

Tax on rental income: By default a non-resident pays 30% of gross rent (or a lower treaty rate), withheld at source, or can elect to treat the rent as business income and pay graduated rates on net income by filing Form 1040-NR and giving Form W-8ECI to the withholding agent.

## Bali, Phuket, Tulum or Batumi? 400 new builds scored side by side

Median price, price per m², distance to the sea and facilities for 400 new-build projects. Batumi is the cheapest by far; Tulum is the furthest from the beach.

RealHunt Research · 2026-10-06

We keep a Top 100 of new-build projects in four places where foreigners buy holiday and rental homes: Bali, Phuket, Tulum and Batumi. This month we gave each of the 400 projects ten scores from 0 to 100. Here is what the four markets look like side by side.

Destination | Median price | Median €/m² | Under €100k | Median distance to sea | Within 1 km of sea | Ready now | Pool | Gym
[Batumi](https://realhunt.co/top/batumi) | €48,630 | €1,358 | 88 | 650 m | 73 | 34 | 56 | 44
[Bali](https://realhunt.co/top/bali) | €153,555 | €1,871 | 24 | 1.5 km | 41 | 64 | 93 | 64
[Tulum](https://realhunt.co/top/tulum) | €146,927 | €2,835 | 9 | 2.7 km | 6 | 1 | 98 | 13
[Phuket](https://realhunt.co/top/phuket) | €159,134 | €3,658 | 14 | 1.0 km | 50 | 45 | 94 | 59

Counts are out of 100 projects in each ranking.

### Cheapest: Batumi, by far

The median Batumi project starts at €48,630, about a third of the other three. 88 of its 100 projects start under €100,000, against 24 in Bali, 14 in Phuket and 9 in Tulum. Most are apartments in towers along the seafront, and 73 are within 1 km of the sea.

### Most expensive per m²: Phuket

Phuket's median is about €3,658 per m², almost double Bali (€1,871). In exchange, Phuket buildings list the most facilities after Bali: 94 have a pool and 59 a gym.

### Furthest from the beach: Tulum

The median Tulum project is 2.7 km from the sea in a straight line, and only 6 of 100 are within 1 km. Most new building is inland in La Veleta, Aldea Zama and Region 15. Tulum is also almost all off-plan: 1 of 100 is ready today, so the developer's track record matters more there than anywhere else.

### Best balance: Bali

Bali has 64 projects ready to move in, 41 within 1 km of the sea and the richest facilities: 93 pools, 64 gyms and 32 coworking spaces. Check the ownership: most foreigners buy leasehold there, and the listing does not always say which it is.

### Pick yours

Every ranking can be filtered and sorted by the ten scores: [Bali](https://realhunt.co/top/bali), [Phuket](https://realhunt.co/top/phuket), [Tulum](https://realhunt.co/top/tulum), [Batumi](https://realhunt.co/top/batumi). We wrote one article per destination too: [Bali](https://realhunt.co/blog/best-new-builds-bali-scored-2026), [Phuket](https://realhunt.co/blog/best-new-builds-phuket-scored-2026), [Tulum](https://realhunt.co/blog/best-new-builds-tulum-scored-2026) and [Batumi](https://realhunt.co/blog/best-new-builds-batumi-scored-2026).

### How the scores work

Every project gets ten scores from 0 to 100: price, value per m², location, beach, facilities, delivery, developer, space, visitor interest and listing detail. The grade of each project is the plain average of the ten. Price, value, space and visitor interest compare a project with the other 99 in the same ranking. Beach uses the straight-line distance to the coastline on OpenStreetMap, and facilities counts what the developer's public listing shows (pool, gym, spa, coworking, security and so on). Those two use the same scale in every destination, so you can compare Bali with Batumi.

None of this is advice to buy. Prices and dates come from public listings and change. Ask the developer before you decide, and check the facilities are built, not only drawn.

### How we pick

A person checks every home before it goes up, and homes that need major work, ruins, bare land and thin listings are turned down. The score then compares each home with every other home on RealHunt, from 70 to 98. Homes already listed in an earlier weekly Top 10 are left out.

Prices are the asking prices when each home was added. Homes sell, so check the listing before you travel.

### How the scores work

Every project gets ten scores from 0 to 100: price, value per m², location, beach, facilities, delivery, developer, space, visitor interest and listing detail. The grade of each project is the plain average of the ten. Price, value, space and visitor interest compare a project with the other 99 in the same ranking. Beach uses the straight-line distance to the coastline on OpenStreetMap, and facilities counts what the developer's public listing shows (pool, gym, spa, coworking, security and so on). Those two use the same scale in every destination, so you can compare Bali with Batumi.

None of this is advice to buy. Prices and dates come from public listings and change. Ask the developer before you decide, and check the facilities are built, not only drawn.

### How the scores work

Every project gets ten scores from 0 to 100: price, value per m², location, beach, facilities, delivery, developer, space, visitor interest and listing detail. The grade of each project is the plain average of the ten. Price, value, space and visitor interest compare a project with the other 99 in the same ranking. Beach uses the straight-line distance to the coastline on OpenStreetMap, and facilities counts what the developer's public listing shows (pool, gym, spa, coworking, security and so on). Those two use the same scale in every destination, so you can compare Bali with Batumi.

None of this is advice to buy. Prices and dates come from public listings and change. Ask the developer before you decide, and check the facilities are built, not only drawn.
